Credit: Krzysztof Bubel / Shutterstock.com. · Retail Insight Network · Krzysztof Bubel / Shutterstock.com. Shubhendu Vimal July 17, 2026 2 min read ZAB.WA 3382.T 7-Eleven Japan's parent company Seven & i Holdings is holding advanced discussions to acquire a stake in Polish convenience store chain Zabka Group, reported Nikkei Asia. Established in 1998, Zabka runs a network of 10,000 franchised outlets across Poland, focusing on food offerings such as coffee and hot snacks. Seven & i is looking to purchase a holding of several tens of percent in Zabka, buying from a mix of investment funds and existing shareholders. The transaction is estimated to be valued at several hundred billion yen, translating to a sum in the hundreds of millions of dollars at a rate of Y100bn ($616m). The move forms part of Seven & i's push to grow its convenience store operations abroad, with the Zabka stake intended to give it an entry point into the Eastern European market. Zabka trades on the Warsaw Stock Exchange and posted revenue of 27.15bn zlotys ($7.16bn) for the year to December 2025. Seven & i has been ramping up its international expansion in recent years and is targeting a rise in its total store count, spanning Japan and other markets, from 87,000 to 100,000 by the end of the decade. At present, the group's presence is heavily weighted towards Japan and North America, with its European footprint limited to approximately 360 outlets across Nordic countries, including Denmark and Norway. A stake in Zabka would substantially widen Seven & i's store network across Europe. Should it proceed, the agreement would represent Seven & i's first significant investment in a convenience store business overseas in half a decade, setting aside its purchase of Convenience Group Holdings, the Australian operator running 7-Eleven-branded stores in that country. Seven & i's last major overseas move of this scale came in 2021, when it acquired Speedway, a US chain combining convenience stores with fuel stations, in a $21bn deal. Separately, Seven & i posted operating income of Y105bn for its first quarter, marking a 122.4% year-on-year increase on a like-for-like basis. Net income attributable to owners of the parent rose 95.3% to Y60.6bn for the three months to 31 May 2026 while earnings per share climbed 118.4% to Y26.21. https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-p.text: BERLIN — Europe is scrambling for more Patriot interceptors to donate to an increasingly desperate Ukraine, which is racing to reinforce its ballistic missile defenses before Russia’s expected winter assault. Kyiv is seeking hundreds of interceptors, but new production will come too late, the war with Iran has strained U.S. supplies, and several of Ukraine’s leading European backers say they have few left that they can safely donate. “Over the last few months, Russia fires more missiles a week at us than we get from partners over months," former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said last week . In July, Ukrainian air defense intercepted only 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles, with another 40 failing to reach their targets, Ukraine's defense ministry said . Advertisement Advertisement Germany, one of Ukraine’s top military aid donors, has already transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. But Berlin must now balance Kyiv’s increasingly urgent needs against the minimum stocks required to protect Germany and meet its NATO commitments. Other European countries are also weighing whether to hang on to their interceptors or give them to Ukraine. “We are really reaching our limits here,” Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, a senior German defense ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin shortly after last month’s NATO summit in Ankara. “We also have to ensure our own protection.” Berlin and other Northern European capitals have urged counterparts elsewhere on the continent to examine what more military equipment and financial support they could release. “I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO. “All the European countries have to step up.” That's putting pressure on countries with stocks of Patriot interceptors like Poland, Spain and Greece. The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles, which are among Ukraine’s few effective defenses against fast-moving Russian ballistic weapons. Ukraine can use other, often cheaper, air-defense systems against drones and cruise missiles. The country is racing to develop its homegrown Freyja interceptor, but the anti-ballistic system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can fill that role. Advertisement Advertisement Until Freyja is ready, Ukraine needs an immediate answer to Russia’s ballistic missiles. “One of the priority directions is Patriot — PAC-3 or PAC-2,” Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told POLITICO. “The first [solution] is buying, or receiving from stockpiles, PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors.” Stuck in Washington The Patriot dependence makes U.S. President Donald Trump essential to Kyiv: Most PAC-3 interceptors are produced in America, which means their sale and any production deals are subject to White House decisions. During Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's meeting with Trump last month, “The main topic was Patriot interceptors,” according to a senior official familiar with the talks. Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump speak on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 8, 2026. | Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images Trump raised hopes at the Ankara summit when he said Ukraine would be allowed to produce U.S.-designed Patriot interceptors under license — a step that could eventually reduce Kyiv’s dependence on scarce American deliveries. U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker made clear that production would not solve the immediate shortage. “A long-term production agreement will not be concluded before this winter,” he told Fox Business, and manufacturing the first missiles would take longer still. Advertisement Advertisement But Trump has now walked that back, last week saying: "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology." Following a Reuters report that the U.S. had almost exhausted its missile stocks thanks to the war against Iran, Trump is now focusing on rebuilding U.S. supplies. Asked on Thursday about Zelenskyy’s calls for more Patriot missiles, he said: “We want missiles too.” Ukraine has also signed a deal to get PAC-2 interceptors being made in Germany, but they are unlikely to arrive before next year. Faced with a shortage of interceptors, Kyiv is now looking at a more aggressive campaign to hit Russian launchers. "The Russians must understand that a few minutes after the launch, the entire team that launches the rocket must die from our ballistic missile," Fedorov said. Europe’s unbalanced effort That puts the immediate burden on Europe, where allies are once again searching their own arsenals — and one another’s — for interceptors that could reach Ukraine before winter. Advertisement Advertisement Germany supplied three Patriot systems from its own military stocks and subsequently arranged two more through a deal under which the U.S. would replenish the Bundeswehr. The Netherlands assembled the components for another complete system, including five launchers, a radar and missiles. But with stocks now stretched thin, governments face limits of their own. Warsaw confirmed in July that it had released several PAC-3 interceptors after requests from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and senior U.S. commanders. Polish outlet Defence24 reported that just five missiles were transferred. Mark Rutte speaks at a press conference ahead of a NATO summit in Ankara on July 6, 2026. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images Even that triggered a political backlash. Opposition lawmakers accused the government of weakening the country’s defenses at a time when Russian missiles and drones have repeatedly strayed across its border. Countries closer to Russia are now becoming less likely to give up existing Patriots because their armed forces already regarded their air defenses as insufficient for national requirements, according to a European diplomat granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic contacts. That is shifting attention toward Southern European countries, which have contributed less to Ukraine than Germany and many Northern European donors. Advertisement Advertisement Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez confirmed in 2024 that Madrid was sending missiles to Ukraine, but the government has not disclosed their type or amount. Spain's defense ministry did not respond to a question from POLITICO whether it had recently been approached for more interceptors or was considering another transfer. It instead pointed to Spain’s wider military support for Ukraine and its NATO commitments. Greece — which traditionally sees fellow NATO member Turkey as its greatest security threat — has not announced any Patriot transfers to Ukraine. Greek media reported in July that Ukraine had requested as many as 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Athens. The Greek defense ministry did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment. Prying open Europe’s arsenals This isn’t the first time European allies have had to cobble together Patriot missile deliveries from their own limited stocks. At a February meeting, Ukraine's Fedorov said he and Rutte worked through a list of interceptors held by European allies, asking governments for whatever they could spare. Advertisement “Dear defense minister of Poland, can you give us five?” Fedorov recalled in this week's interview. Berlin offered to top up the effort. “If you get 20 out of all the countries, I'll give you an extra five,” Fedorov quoted German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius as saying. “That’s the exercise we had to perform to get more than 20. And it is a hard mission.” Kyiv is continuing those types of talks with its allies. “Of course, Ukrainian diplomats have been working with Spain, Greece and everyone in the world who has [PACs],” said the senior official familiar with the talks. “Everything depends on the U.S., and the lack of political will to help influences everyone else.” “The American administration could have helped, but they don’t do this. And as the result it’s been hard with everyone else,” they added. For Kyiv, the arguments over allied stockpiles are unfolding against a ticking clock. With demand for PAC-3 interceptors surging in the Middle East, the Pentagon replenishing its own stock and many European countries worrying about their own ability to fend off a future Russian attack, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was struggling to buy, exchange or secure any available rounds. “We are literally fighting for every missile,” Sybiha said. Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv. Advertisement

Beállítom Donald Trump szerdán azt mondta, hogy nagyszerű beszélgetést folytatott Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnökkel, és megismételte azt az állítását, hogy szerinte az orosz vezető kész megállapodást kötni az ukrajnai háború befejezéséről – írja a CBS . „Megállapodást akar kötni. https://www.aol.com/articles/live-paris-.text: Djena Camara Thu, September 10, 2026 at 3:01 PM UTC 0 Hvar, Croatia, is one of the cities I recommend visiting in Europe.Dreamer4787/Shutterstock I've been living in Europe for a few years, and have tried to visit as many cities as possible. I enjoyed spending time in places like Prague and Hvar, Croatia, and can't wait to return. However, I was a little disappointed by my visits to Marseille, France, and Stockholm. One of the biggest perks of living in Europe for the past few years has been the ease of hopping on a flight to explore new destinations. During my time here, I've visited 26 cities in countries like France, Portugal, Iceland, Croatia, Sweden, and the Czech Republic. Each destination brought something unique to the table, but unfortunately, not every experience lived up to my expectations. Here are the four cities I'd return to in a heartbeat — and two I'd probably skip next time. I loved visiting Faro, Portugal. Digitalsignal/Getty Images Located in the Algarve region of Portugal , Faro is a vacation hot spot with gorgeous beaches, unique architecture, and a relaxed atmosphere. One of the highlights of my trip was walking along the cliffs for an hour with a friend to find a secluded beach. The views were magical, and the experience felt like something out of a dream. Faro's warm weather and welcoming charm make it a place I'd gladly return to. Prague felt like a fairytale. Pauline Lewis/Getty Images In my opinion, Prague's fairytale-like architecture, vibrant nightlife, and rich history make it a top contender for one of Europe's most beautiful cities. Walking through Old Town Square feels like stepping back in time, and every corner of the city holds something fascinating. The food scene is also worth mentioning — traditional Czech dishes like goulash and trdelník (chimney cake) are must-try items. Despite spending a few days there, I felt like I barely scratched the surface of what the city has to offer. Hvar, Croatia, is unlike anywhere else I've been. xbrchx/Getty Images Croatia is a dream for beach lovers, and the island of Hvar was definitely a highlight of my trip. Hvar combines charming cobblestone streets, fantastic restaurants, and dreamy beaches with crystal-clear water. Advertisement The surrounding smaller islands are just as stunning, offering secluded spots to relax and unwind. On this trip, I stepped out of my comfort zone by visiting a nude beach, and even made new friends who shared my love for exploring. Hvar's blend of adventure and relaxation has earned it a permanent spot on my list of favorite European travel destinations . I'd happily revisit Reykjavik, Iceland. Tsuguliev/Shutterstock Iceland is known as being a pricy tourist destination, but my visit was worth every penny. The capital, Reykjavik, is packed with charm and incredibly walkable. The local cuisine, including fresh seafood and lamb, was some of the best I've had in Europe. What stood out the most, though, were the unplanned magical moments. One night, after leaving a karaoke bar, I looked up to see the northern lights dancing across the sky. It was an awe-inspiring experience that felt almost surreal. That kind of spontaneous magic makes Iceland a place I'd visit again and again. However, I'm not rushing to return to Marseille, France. Steve Lorillere/Getty Images Although France is brimming with beauty and culture, my visit to Marseille felt a bit lackluster. The city's architecture is undeniably stunning, but Marseille seemed to lack anything that made it truly special. Exploring the city can also be a workout — it's very hilly, and unless you're prepared for a lot of uphill walking, it can be a bit exhausting. Next time, I'd prioritize neighboring French spots like Aix-en-Provence or Nice instead. Unfortunately, Stockholm didn't live up to my expectations. Angel Villalba/Getty Images I had heard so much about Stockholm and couldn't wait to visit. However, I left feeling a bit underwhelmed. The city is undeniably beautiful, with its waterways and historic buildings, but it lacked the spark I hoped for. After visiting a few other Nordic cities, Stockholm just felt a bit monotonous. http://www.enterstageright.com/archive/a.text: home > archive > 2026 > this article A quick glance at fashion, cosmetics, and cosmetology in Poland By Mark Wegierski web posted September 21, 2026 These are memories of a happier time in East-Central Europe, twenty-three years ago. Poland is a country where the fashion sense and interest in cosmetology of many women is perhaps the third-highest in Europe (after France and Italy). Already during the later Communist era, it was said that women in Polandâs large cities would adopt the fashions of Paris a few days after their appearance in the West. Also, many Polish women tend to visit their âkosmetyczkaâ (cosmetician) at the beauty salon or aesthetics center with a frequency somewhat greater than that seen in Anglo-American societies. I gained some knowledge of this whole scene through my female relative â herself a tall, lithe, brown-eyed brunette who might have appeared to some observers as looking like a former model -- who had been working in the cosmetological profession for over twenty years. Unlike in Anglo-American societies, there are extensive programs of study at the university level in cosmetology in Poland. My relative, having the appropriate university training and decades of experience, rather lamented the fact that standards in the profession appear to be dropping, with some cosmetological study programs lasting a mere three months. I recall that on Sunday, September 21, 2003, during my visit to Poland, I travelled with her to Warsaw, in her compact but elegant Peugeot 206, to attend a large trade show for cosmetologists. It was a sunny and rather warm day. I had been staying at Ciechocinek, which is a spa and resort town of about 14,000 permanent residents. It is known for its unique titration towers â large wooden structures with thick layers of bramble, through which water from nearby salt springs is filtered into the air, producing a healthy microclimate, approximating that of sea-air. Ciechocinek lies about 200 kilometers northwest of the capital. We drove into Warsaw along the Wislostrada (Vistula Highway) which lies to the east of the main city of Warsaw, along the Vistula River. We found the trade center with some difficulty, and there were literally hundreds of cars parked on the sides of the road as we drove up toward the huge building. My relative was able to skillfully find a parking spot in the vast underground garage, despite the bustle of the place. The trade center had probably been built only a few years ago. Warsaw is clearly the most prosperous city in Poland, with a huge building boom. While this is great for Warsaw itself, there are still the much poorer regions and smaller towns of Poland, especially in the southeast of the country, that are hoping for some relief from their often-grinding poverty and unemployment. The official unemployment rate in the country as a whole had been around twenty percent for several years in the 1990s and early 2000s. We finally rushed up into the trade center venue, a vast hall jam-packed with exhibitors and huge crowds. My relative expressed the opinion that admission to the trade show should have been more selective (i.e., only for recognized professionals). As it was, anyone who paid 15 zlotys was allowed inside, resulting in a virtual mob scene. The cosmetology-related products, devices, and furniture on display were of an enormous variety, and the prices for some of the items were out of this world, e.g., several thousand Euros for a professional salon bed. I gained some insight into how expensive getting effectively set up in this profession could be. My relative insisted on viewing virtually every exhibit in the trade show, but after an exhaustive and exhausting run-through, which included picking up various brochures and pamphlets, we stepped out the door. We thought of eating at the local cafeteria in the trade center building, but the crowds there were massive, too. We slipped out of the âmadhouseâ and drove up in light Sunday traffic to Three Crossesâ Square (Plac Trzech Krzyzy) which is in the Downtown-South part of Warsaw, where there was a fine restaurant with which she was familiar. Walking to the restaurant, called Modulor CafÃ© Bar, we noted the bright whiteness of the freshly restored church at the center of the square; the ponderous-looking, cavernous modern hotel (the Warsaw Sheraton, I believe); as well as the trendy student hang-out, Szpilki Szparki Szpulki (Needles, eyes, threads). Eating at the Modulor restaurant at about six oâclock in the evening, it was mostly empty, but I imagine it is rather jumping later in the evening, as it also seems to want to cater to a trendy clientele. There is a large bar alongside part of the right wall of the restaurant, the tables are of black marble color, and there are various framed caricatures of persons active in the Warsaw arts scene â some of them probably from earlier decades -- on the walls. The food â such as roast strips of chicken on a bed of lettuce -- was excellent tasting, with the added bonus that you could order things like real milkshakes (i.e., something frothy that can be sipped rather than slurped). Except in major and medium sized cities, and a few smaller centers, very high-quality restaurants in Poland are not that easy to find, presumably because the cooking at home is usually so good, and it has been estimated that the average Polish person eats only 1 in 30 meals at a restaurant (although this may have begun to change to more out-of-home dining in more recent years). Having rested up, we returned to our car, to begin our over three-hour trip back to Ciechocinek. Unfortunately, a large, prosperous middle-class has not yet arisen in Poland, and it is that class of women that would probably give the largest support to cosmetology. Indeed, in the aftermath of Communism, a small number of people have become very rich, while wide swathes of the population have been pauperized. Ironically, some people look back with comparative fondness at the so-called âgolden yearsâ of the Gierek era of the 1970s, when small luxuries appeared to be within greater reach of the average pocketbook. (An earlier version of this article has appeared in Polonez: Canadian-Polish News (December 2006), p. 13.) Mark Wegierski is a Toronto-based writer and historical researcher. He was born in Toronto of Polish immigrant parents. Home Home Print this page

https://kcrr.com/ixp/675/p/cedar-rapids-.text: New Sculpture Park Planned for Mays Island in Cedar Rapids New Sculpture Park Planned for Mays Island in Cedar Rapids Ryan "Brain" Brainard Ryan "Brain" Brainard Published: October 16, 2026 Courtlin Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A new public space is planned for Mays Island in Cedar Rapids that will combine art, nature, and the community. The Cedar Rapids Bank & Trust Sculpture Park On October 15th, the city of Cedar Rapids announced a partnership with Cedar Rapids Bank & Trust, whose lead gift will help bring the signature artwork to Mays Island. The Cedar Rapids Bank & Trust Sculpture Park will be a free public space where residents can come and enjoy art along the riverfront and enjoy time outdoors at one of the city's most recognizable places. Cedar Rapids Bank & Trust made the announcement in conjunction with the company's 25th anniversary. When Will the Project Begin? According to the City of Cedar Rapids , the selection of the park's anchor artwork will start now and wrap up in 2027. Development and site preparation will also begin. In 2027, improvement projects on Mays Island will begin, including; Renovating the entry plaza and redesigning the canopy. An accessible sidewalk network Coordinated signage, lighting, and amenities. The city stated that it plans to unveil the anchor artwork for the park in 2028, which will help mark 20 years of progress and recovery since the flood of 2008.
